sources.claim: The optional linked-account impersonation method requires both the KSA annotation and an IAM allow binding for the namespace/KSA member. Access to target Google Cloud resources remains a separate authorization requirement. The fixture declares this method and does not imply all Workload Identity Federation configurations require an IAM service account.

Troubleshooting distinguishes Kubernetes API RBAC authorization from Workload Identity Federation authentication. The workload-pool, metadata-service and account-link observations matter; a Google API permission denial is not itself a Kubernetes RBAC failure.

Workload Identity Federation provides workload authentication to Google Cloud APIs and can use service-account impersonation. Authentication and target-resource IAM authorization are separate checks; successful credential acquisition does not imply access to every resource.

k8s_container identifies project, location, cluster, namespace, Pod and container. IAM and storage extracts are separately labelled owner-supplied observations in this packet rather than claimed container-log fields.

a.conclusion: The Pod selects the expected KSA, but its annotation points to rules-audit rather than the intended rules-reader IAM account. The observed impersonation denial targets that wrong account before object access. This establishes a link mismatch, not a storage-read denial for the intended principal or a Kubernetes RBAC failure.

The IAM owner confirms the existing namespace-specific impersonation binding and intended account with the storage owner before the owners select a narrow approved correction.

unsupported: Calling the observed error a storage.objects.get denial for rules-reader when the request failed earlier against rules-audit.
Claiming Kubernetes RBAC, node identity or a cluster-admin role is the demonstrated cause or repair.
Requesting credentials/tokens, editing the annotation, broadening grants or claiming the mapping correction guarantees full recovery.
unknowns: When and why the annotation diverged from the intended mapping.

b.conclusion: The selected KSA, annotation and namespace-specific impersonation binding agree, and acquisition succeeded for rules-reader. The subsequent object read is denied for storage.objects.get under that principal. The supplied absence of an applicable allow supports a target-resource authorization gap, with other policy effects still for the owner to assess.
next_checks: Jordan asks the storage and IAM owners to compare the exact principal, object and permission with approved access intent, effective allows and deny/organization constraints at the incident time.
The owners decide a least-privilege correction through the existing change process if access is intended; no broad project role or Kubernetes RBAC change follows from this evidence.
Obtain a sanitized successful object-read receipt and sustained rules refresh outcomes after any approved correction; do not request or display credentials.
unsupported: Diagnosing a wrong KSA-to-IAM mapping or failed impersonation while ignoring successful acquisition for the expected account.
Treating successful authentication as proof of object authorization or Kubernetes RBAC as controlling the Cloud Storage permission.
Granting project Editor, cluster-admin or broad storage access, requesting tokens, or asserting that one missing allow excludes all other policy effects.
unknowns: The intended object-level access scope and permission-change history.
Whether deny policies or organization constraints also matter, and whether any proposed correction restores sustained refreshes.
